video_title: The $300 Billion Structured Notes Market Is Booming | Odd Lots
gist: Nomura's Alex Micalizzi explains how autocallable and worst-of structured notes work, why US SEC-registered issuance is heading to about $300B, and how dealers hedging them leaves vega and gamma exposures that can amplify moves in drift-down or rebounding markets.

insights.claim: A structured note is effectively a bank IOU plus a derivative: the investor lends the issuer $100, forgoes interest and takes issuer credit risk, and receives customized equity exposure such as a call spread, a put spread, or a yield funded by selling a put.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Yield notes are short-put positions in disguise; the coupon is premium income, not free money.
insights.quote: you give the issuer $100, and you're forgoing an interest rate, and in return, you take the issuer's credit risk

insights.claim: Natural buyers of bank structured products are predominantly high net worth individuals via the private bank, who want yield and downside protection versus owning linear stock and cannot replicate worst-of correlation structures in listed markets.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Retail-wealth demand for yield is the flow source behind dealer vega supply.
insights.quote: Predominantly high net worth individuals through the private bank.

insights.claim: An autocallable terminates early if the underlying is above its initial level on periodic observation dates; this lets the issuer pay a higher coupon than on a plain put because the put becomes worthless in rallies, so the investor takes a contingent bet.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Autocall yield is paid for giving up the upside and taking reinvestment risk.

insights.claim: Autocallable investors face reinvestment risk: they enter when implied vol is high and coupons rich, but if markets rally and vol falls, the note knocks out and the next coupon available is lower, similar to convexity in mortgages.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Spot-up/vol-down punishes note holders; spot-down-slowly/vol-high is their ideal.

insights.claim: A typical knock-in structure example: a 60% strike on a one-year note observed quarterly means investors keep protection until the index is down 40%, but below that they take the full downside from $100, so risk of losing the entire amount justifies a higher coupon than a vanilla put.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Buffers are cliff-like, creating binary digital exposure that dealers must hedge.

insights.claim: Worst-of autocallables on S&P, Nasdaq and Russell generate more premium than single-index notes because the worst performer determines the payoff, but they add correlation risk the dealer must model and hedge.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Correlation risk is priced opaquely; dealers carry it.

insights.claim: SEC-registered US structured notes are on track to reach about $300 billion issuance this year versus about $200 billion last year, with the biggest growth in worst-of autocallables on S&P, Nasdaq and Russell.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: A 50% annual jump makes this a first-order driver of long-dated index vol supply.
insights.quote: SEC registered notes this year on track to hit about 300 billion versus, approximately 200 billion last year

insights.claim: The Russell's multi-year sideways trend followed by a straight-line rally since Liberation Day has knocked out many Russell-linked worst-of autocalls, so volumes recycle and notional rises every time notes redeem and are reissued.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Rising markets raise gross issuance via knock-out churn, not just new demand.

insights.claim: Single-stock structured notes (Nvidia, Apple, Meta, semis, hyperscalers, neo-clouds like CoreWeave) offer very high yields, with a Bloomberg column citing around 40% annualized, and observe knock-outs daily rather than quarterly.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: AI-name notes are a leveraged-yield way to express AI views; the yields signal high implied vol.

insights.claim: Structured note markets are far bigger and older in Asia, where the products started in Japan when rates went to zero as a way to enhance yield; US notes are more participation- and income-oriented.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: US issuance is more likely to be used as dividend-like income, so US behavior may converge toward Asia if sideways markets persist.

insights.claim: Dealers hedge notes by first neutralizing delta, then assigning vega to the put at the expected-life horizon and selling listed or broker-market downside to S&P market makers; this is an imperfect hedge because the knock-out digitals are call spreads that cannot be replicated at notional size.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Hedges are approximate; mismatches show up as vega and gamma risks when markets move.

insights.claim: When markets fall, notes that would have knocked out extend toward their 3-5 year maturities, so dealers must hedge more long-dated vega just as listed-market counterparties and IDB participants pull back, leaving them selling optionality into weak demand.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Falling markets create concentrated supply of long-dated vol, pressuring implied vol term structure.

insights.claim: If markets rebound sharply after dealers hedged an extended life, notes knock out in months and dealers are left short vega on the street with no new autocallable supply to offset, a squeeze in long-dated vol.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: V-shaped recoveries can produce vega squeezes; the product dynamic is a potential cause of spot-up vol-up.

insights.claim: Micalizzi agrees this structured-note vega dynamic contributes to Charlie McElligott's spot-up vol-up regime, more prevalent in single stocks but visible in longer-dated index options due to worst-of and SEC-registered note growth.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Structured-note flows help explain why implied vol stays elevated near all-time highs.

insights.claim: A large buyer of upside call options used to protect portfolios disappeared as portfolios shrank in the selloff, removing a natural counterparty for dealer vega just as supply rose.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Counterparty demand for vol is cyclical and procyclical with equity drawdowns.

insights.claim: Daily-observation single-stock worst-of notes create an on/off market: each day the dealer may have no option at all or a large put, which pins hedging to skew and makes the books extremely binary.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Single-stock skew and gap risk can move abruptly on the notes' observation mechanics.

insights.claim: Near knock-in barriers or digital knock-out levels, dealers can flip to short gamma, which means buying as markets rise and selling as they fall, exacerbating moves near those levels.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Large structured-note barriers can act as accelerants around specific price levels.

insights.claim: Micalizzi says the market has not yet really tested notes near knock-in levels, so fingerprints are seen more at knock-outs because those occur quarterly rather than once every one to five years.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Knock-in-driven gamma is an untested tail risk in a real bear market.

insights.claim: A slow grind lower with falling vol and flattening skew can hurt dealers who hedged with spreads, because local hedges fail on large moves while the notes retain value beyond the spread's payout.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Both slow grinds and crashes hurt; the benign quiet drift-down is best only for note holders.

insights.claim: Local-vol models underestimate the forward-starting relationships in quarterly knock-out structures, so dealers use stochastic vol, which depends on vol-of-vol that is hard to observe outside VIX options and impossible for single stocks.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Model risk is meaningful and likely priced into coupons.

insights.claim: Structured-product innovation follows pain: after the 2018 drift-down hurt dealers, knock-in-knock-out products emerged, which solved one problem but created secondary issues.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Expect new exotic features to follow the current episode, with new hidden risks.

insights.claim: An exotic single-stock worst-of structure lets a stock be permanently knocked out once it is above its barrier even if it falls later, leaving a deep in-the-money put on the remaining names that can vanish if the last stock rallies, creating a massive vol-of-wall position for dealers.
insights.speaker: Alex Micalizzi (Nomura)
insights.so_what: Path-dependent exotics concentrate risk in sudden binary events.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway note AI-related assets are in turbulence, with neo-clouds weak and credit default swaps on large companies including Nvidia inching up, just as structured notes provide leveraged ways to bet on or hedge AI.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Stress in AI credit adds to the case that structured-note flows could amplify an AI repricing.
